About

Hi there!

I'm a student at San José State University focused on software engineering for machine learning and AI. I like building things end to end: cleaning the data, training and testing the model, and shipping it as an app people can actually use.

My latest project predicts student dropout risk with scikit-learn and Keras, audits the model for fairness with Fairlearn and SHAP, and runs as a live Streamlit app. I also write SQL in DuckDB to turn raw event data into product metrics. I care most about AI that is reliable, fair, and easy to explain.

Before college, I spent four and a half years teaching kids to code in JavaScript, C#, and Godot at Code Ninjas, and I helped run a college-level machine learning course at UC Berkeley's ATDP. Teaching made me better at writing clear code and explaining hard ideas simply. I speak English, Telugu, and Spanish.

Blog

Notes from the field

Oct 2026·Event recap·3 min read

Two days at The AI Conference in San Francisco

On September 30 and October 1, I attended The AI Conference in San Francisco with Girls Who Code SJSU. Over two days of keynotes, breakout sessions, and talks, I heard from researchers, engineers, and founders at companies like Anthropic, Uber, Target, and Intuit about where AI is headed.

LLM evaluationInterpretabilityAI agentsData curation

A few sessions that stuck with me:

On evaluating AI in production

Sowmya Podila introduced SERA, a 21-metric LLM-as-a-judge framework that runs multi-turn persona simulations and gates deployments through CI/CD, scoring safety by the worst turn and quality by the average. Dharmin Parikh and Himaanshu Gupta showed how Uber calibrates LLM judges against human review to catch responses that are fluent but not grounded in real-time data.

On how models work and what makes them better

Emmanuel Ameisen from Anthropic walked through interpretability research showing that models learn shared representations of concepts across languages and modalities. Ari Morcos from DatologyAI argued that data curation, through filtering, deduplication, and algorithmic mixing, is the most underinvested lever for improving models at a fixed compute budget.

On building agents that hold up

Vidya Meenakshi Kambhampati from Intuit shared lessons from a stateful multi-agent system: put constraints in Pydantic field descriptions so they reach the LLM untruncated, write error messages specific enough for agents to self-correct, and design checkpoints that recover from mid-execution failures.

One of my biggest takeaways was seeing how much goes into building a reliable AI system beyond simply choosing or training a model. Data quality, evaluation, interpretability, grounding, failure recovery, and thoughtful system design all matter.

Thank you to all the speakers for sharing your work. Hearing how teams actually build, test, and improve AI in the real world gave me a much clearer picture of the field. Attending with Sreya Mathew and Emily Chou made it even better. I'm grateful we got to learn and explore together. I'm incredibly grateful to Girls Who Code SJSU for the opportunity to attend The AI Conference, and for two days of learning, growing, and connecting with people who are passionate about AI.
